title: Longest Brick That Builds Both Strings
statement:
Say a string b builds a string s when s is b written one or more times back to back. For example "XY" builds "XYXYXY", but it does not build "XYX".

Given two strings s1 and s2, return the longest string that builds both of them. If no string builds both, return the empty string "".

examples.why: "XY" three times gives s1 and twice gives s2. "XYXY" builds s2 but not s1.
"A" builds both, but so does "AA", and we want the longest. Its length is gcd(4, 6) = 2.
Both start with "AB", but nothing repeated builds "ABA" and "ABAB" at the same time.

hints: If a brick builds both strings, its length must divide both lengths. Which lengths are even possible?
If any brick exists, then s1 + s2 and s2 + s1 are the same string, because both are just the brick repeated. Check that first.
When s1 + s2 equals s2 + s1, the answer is the prefix of s1 whose length is gcd(len(s1), len(s2)).

explain.intuition:
A brick that builds s1 must have a length that divides len(s1), and the same for s2. So its length divides g = gcd(len(s1), len(s2)). You could try every such length, but there is a neater test.

If some brick b builds both, then s1 + s2 and s2 + s1 are both b repeated the same number of times, so they are equal. The converse is also true: if the two concatenations are equal, the strings share a common brick, and the longest one is the first g characters of s1. Any shorter common brick would build that prefix too, so the gcd-length one is always the longest.
steps: Compute g = gcd(s1.length, s2.length) with Euclid's algorithm.
pitfalls: Returning the shortest common brick ("A") instead of the longest ("AA").
Checking only that the prefixes agree. "ABAB" and "ABA" share a prefix but no brick.
Assuming the shorter string is itself the answer. In the second example, "AAAA" does not build "AAAAAA".

solutions.title: Try every prefix length, longest first
solutions.idea: For each length from min(n, m) down to 1 that divides both lengths, check whether that prefix of s1 builds both strings.

solutions.title: Concatenation check + gcd of lengths
solutions.idea: A common brick exists exactly when s1 + s2 equals s2 + s1. Then the longest brick is the prefix of length gcd(n, m).

followups: Return the shortest brick that builds a single string s. How do you find it in O(n)?
Extend the answer to a list of k strings.
